chapter_theme: The benediction that opens the epic: three-line venbas hail the moon, the sun, the rain and Puhar, each for being like the Chola's umbrella, wheel, grace and line; the narrative then calls Puhar a city the learned never speak of as declining, introduces Kannaki at twelve and Kovalan at sixteen as children of its two great merchant houses, and tells their wedding, with the Vedic circling of the fire, the women's blessing that she never be parted from her lover, and a closing praise of the Chola's wheel.

the aged Brahmin priest who conducts the wedding rite

the unnamed Chola king of Puhar, praised as சென்னி, காவிரி நாடன், செம்பியன்

silappathikaram:1:1-12.reading: Four short venbas each hail a power twice, the moon, the sun, the great rain and the city Puhar, and give as the reason for praising each that it resembles the Chola: the moon his cool white umbrella sheltering the world, the sun his wheel of rule circling Meru, the rain his bounty pouring on the sea-girt earth, and Puhar his lineage rising and spreading.
silappathikaram:1:1-12.nuance: The comparison runs backwards from the usual royal praise: the king is not likened to the sun and moon, the heavenly bodies are praised because they are like the king (the ablative ஆன் of அளித்தலான், திரிதலான், சுரத்தலான், ஒழுகலான் gives the reason). The opening worship names no god; nature and the city stand where an invocation would be, and the king is in every stanza without being named except by the titles சென்னி and காவிரி நாடன்.

claims.claim: a king's bounty sustains the world as the rain does

silappathikaram:1:13-29.reading: The narrator says that the learned, whatever they say of Pothiyil, the Himalaya or Puhar of the ancient families who never leave it, speak of these only as standing unshaken and never of their decline, and in that city he introduces the twelve-year-old daughter of the merchant Maanaaygan, Kannaki, whom women worship as Lakshmi's beauty and the faultless northern star's virtue.
silappathikaram:1:13-29.nuance: Puhar is set beside two mountains as a thing that does not move, and the claim is given to the wise of complete learning (முடித்த கேள்வி முழுதுணர்ந்தோர்), so the epic opens on a confidence in the city's permanence that its sequel will undo. Kannaki is first named by her father's house and by others' praise: she does nothing in the unit, and the star of the faultless wife (வடமீன், the Arundhati star) is what women see in her before her story begins. Her name ends the unit with மன்னோ, the particle of something past and lasting.
silappathikaram:1:13-29.event: The narrator introduces Kannaki, twelve-year-old daughter of the merchant Maanaaygan of Puhar.

silappathikaram:1:30-44.reading: The narrator introduces Kovalan, sixteen, son of the merchant Maasaathuvan, master of great wealth who pours out his coming riches for others and whose house stands with the families that the king of the whole earth honours, a youth whom women hail as Murugan come again; then the two fathers, delighting to see them married, set the bride on an elephant's neck and announce the wedding to the city.
silappathikaram:1:30-44.nuance: Both introductions are built alike (அவளுந்தான் / அவனுந்தான், ending பாள்மன்னோ / பான்மன்னோ), so bride and groom are presented as a matched pair of houses before they are persons; Kovalan's praise, though, is all of women's admiration (மதிமுக மடவார், ஆயத்துப் பாராட்டி), a hint of the charm that will draw him to Madhavi. The father's wealth is praised for being given away (வருநிதி பிறர்க்குஆர்த்தும்).
silappathikaram:1:30-44.event: The two fathers arrange Kovalan and Kannaki's marriage and announce it to the city from an elephant's back.

silappathikaram:1:45-68.reading: Drums, conches and the royal umbrella go out as if a king rode forth; under a pearl canopy on diamond pillars, at the hour the moon joins Rohini, Kovalan circles the fire with Kannaki as the aged Brahmin shows the Vedic way, and the adorned women, scattering flowers and blessing her never to part from her lover nor loosen her embrace, seat the Arundhati-like bride on the marriage couch; the unit closes hailing the Chola who set his tiger on the Himalaya and rolls his single wheel everywhere.
silappathikaram:1:45-68.nuance: The women's blessing (காதலற் பிரியாமல் கவவுக்கை ஞெகிழாமல் தீதுஅறுக) names exactly the harm the story will bring: separation and loosened arms. Line 53 exclaims what vow (நோன்பு) the onlookers must have kept to see the circling of the fire, treating the sight as the fruit of past observance. The rite is Vedic in form (மறைவழி, தீவலம்), led by a Brahmin, though the families are merchants. How lines 64 to 68 attach is not plain: தங்கிய and எனவே may make the praise of the Chola part of the women's words, or the poet's own close.
silappathikaram:1:45-68.event: Kovalan and Kannaki are married with the circling of the fire, and the women bless her and lead her to the marriage couch.

links.note: The benediction likens the Chola's bounty to the rain pouring from above; the couplet makes rain itself depend on the king's not bending justice.
links.teaches: Read against the couplet, the opening simile of rain and royal grace is not mere flattery but the old belief that the sky's giving follows the king's justice, which the epic will put to the test when a Pandya's crooked verdict brings fire rather than rain on his city.

gains.a: the simile gains a causal ground: rain and royal grace are linked because a just king's realm is the one the sky waters
gains.b: the couplet's rule gains a ceremonial setting, sung at a wedding as praise rather than stated as a warning

links.note: Both see the king's white umbrella as the moon; the benediction praises the moon for resembling the Chola's sheltering umbrella, the quatrain says every king under such an umbrella has been carried off as dead.
links.teaches: The same moon-umbrella serves the epic's opening as a sign of rule that shelters the world and serves the Naladiyar as proof that such rule ends, so the pair shows the epic beginning in the confidence the ethics book was written to undercut.

gains.a: the hymn's royal moon gains a shadow: the image it uses for lasting shelter is the Naladiyar's stock image of the king who dies
gains.b: the quatrain's umbrella gains an instance of the praise it answers, the court poet's moon that is meant to outlast the king

links.note: The epic opens saying the learned speak of Puhar only as standing unshaken, never of its decline; the Manimekalai tells how the city was swallowed by the sea when the Indra festival was neglected and Manimekala Deivam cursed it.
links.teaches: Taken together, the two epics make the city whose permanence the wise affirm at the first wedding the city the sea takes in the next generation, so the opening's confidence becomes the first instance of the impermanence the sequel preaches.

links.note: Kovalan's father is introduced as the master of great wealth who pours out his riches for others; in the Manimekalai Manimekalai finds him in a Buddhist monastery (பள்ளி) as one who has taken up great austerity (மா தவம்).
links.teaches: The merchant whose giving is praised at his son's wedding ends as a renouncer, so the pair traces in one man the passage from the householder's generosity to the renunciation the Manimekalai holds higher.

links.note: The wedding women bless Kannaki never to be parted from her lover nor loosen her embrace; two kaathais later Kovalan buys Madhavi's garland, cannot leave her and forgets his home.
links.teaches: The blessing names the very loss the story brings within two kaathais, so the wedding song works as an unknowing forecast, and the separation reads as a reversal of a rite performed with fire and Veda.

new_concepts.gloss: the vow; a religious observance or discipline undertaken

source_issues: Lineation: the kaathai has 68 lines as shown against the edition's printed last line 65; the short connecting words set on lines of their own (ஆங்கு, அதனால், அவளுந்தான், அவனுந்தான், அவரை, அவ்வழி) may be counted differently in the edition.
Lines 48 and 62 carry repaired TSCII characters (ு + ட read as ூ); the repaired forms (மாலைதாழ், தீதுஅறுக) read correctly.
Line 46 lacks a space after the comma in பணிலம்,வெண்குடை.

Lines 64 to 68: the syntax joining the women's seating of the bride (ஏற்றினார், தங்கிய) to the closing praise of the Chola (எனவே) is unclear, so whether the praise is the women's or the poet's cannot be fixed.
